title: Clocks Go Back: How Does Your Phone Know the Time Changed?
caption: Your phone doesn't notice the clock change. It follows the time zone database, a rulebook kept by volunteers, and applies it automatically.
pinned_comment: Extra hour of sleep, or just annoying? 👇

lines.text: Clocks go back this weekend. Your phone already knows.
But it doesn't notice anything. It follows a rulebook.
Your phone gets the exact time from your network or from internet time servers.
Those servers are synced to atomic clocks around the world.
But the exact time and your local time are two different things.
The rules for every country's clock changes live in one list, the time zone database.
It's maintained by a small team of volunteers.

visual.label: keep the world's time zone rules

lines.text: Rules can change with only weeks of notice, so the list is updated several times a year.
When a government changes its rules, the new list ships with your phone's next update.
That's why an outdated phone can show the wrong hour after a switch.

right.heading: Fact
right.text: It follows a time zone rulebook

lines.text: In Europe and the UK, clocks go back on the last Sunday of October.
In the US, one week later.
So enjoy the extra hour of sleep on Sunday. And your phone? It knew all along…

sources.title: IANA: Time Zone Database (maintained by volunteers)
